frameworks.name: BATNA Framework
frameworks.definition: Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement; a counter-anchor that establishes your walk-away standard and determines leverage in any negotiation.

frameworks.name: Five Leverage Sources in Negotiation
frameworks.definition: Five domains where BATNA creates negotiating power: personal purchasing (dating/relationships), inventory sales, employment, vendor relationships, and partnership/business acquisition.

claims.text: BATNA (Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement) provides significant negotiating leverage. Research from London Business School found that negotiators who know their alternatives set higher aspirations, make more aggressive first offers, and negotiate better outcomes overall.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Knowing your alternatives anchors your expectations and establishes a decision standard that you only accept deals better than your best alternative.

claims.text: BATNA functions as a psychological power source that is established before sitting down to negotiate. If you sit down and need the deal while having no other options, tactical adjustments during negotiation are ineffective; it is like winning at poker through bluffing alone instead of holding strong cards.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: entering negotiation from position of need
claims.mechanism: Having a strong BATNA removes dependency and shifts negotiating position from weakness to strength; without it, tactical moves fail because the other party perceives your desperation.
bounded_by: Does not apply when you have no credible alternative and the deal is your only option

claims.text: In business acquisition contexts, your BATNA is your ability to keep the existing business running. When selling Gym Launch and Prestige Labs, not needing to sell provided negotiating power because the businesses were generating ongoing revenue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A business that generates cash flow without sale provides an alternative outcome (continued operation) that removes urgency from negotiation.
bounded_by: Does not apply to distressed sales where business is losing money

claims.text: In employment negotiation, having another job offer strengthens your position with an existing employer. You should negotiate with an existing employer only when you already have another offer on the table.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: A competing offer is concrete proof of your market value and removes the employer's position that you have nowhere else to go.
bounded_by: This tactic can only be used a limited number of times before losing goodwill with an employer

claims.text: In vendor negotiations, obtaining multiple bids before deciding creates BATNA by comparing terms. Getting 4-5 vendor quotes educates you on industry terms and allows you to leverage one vendor's offer against another.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Multiple bids show you the market range for services and provide proof that alternatives exist, shifting negotiating position in your favor.
bounded_by: Requires that vendor market is sufficiently competitive to produce real option variation

claims.text: Taking the first offer in any negotiation is a mistake because even if the first offer is optimal within a single negotiation, comparing it against all alternative offers you would receive shows whether the deal is actually competitive.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Accepting the first offer without comparison prevents you from knowing the market-clearing price or whether the offer is above or below market.
bounded_by: Does not apply in monopoly or single-option scenarios where no real alternatives exist

claims.text: When you hold BATNA overtly (stating you have other offers), a counterparty may edge up their offer marginally to compete rather than lose the deal. When you hold BATNA confidently in the back of your mind without stating it, you can negotiate more aggressively because your psychological confidence shifts your anchoring.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Explicit BATNA disclosure triggers defensive marginal concessions; implicit BATNA confidence triggers aggressive counteroffer swings because you project that you will succeed regardless.

claims.text: From a vendor's perspective, if you have 20 other customers and strong demand for your services exceeds your supply capacity, your BATNA is that you do not need any single customer. This supply-demand imbalance flips negotiating leverage to the vendor.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When supply is constrained and demand is high, declining a customer is costless because another customer will replace them at the same or higher terms.
bounded_by: Requires true supply constraint; if actual supply exceeds demand, this leverage disappears

claims.text: On a home purchase negotiation, if the property is aggressively priced and has received no competing bids, the negotiating dynamic becomes 'who wants it less.' The buyer's BATNA (keeping their current home) versus the seller's BATNA (continuing to hold an overpriced property) determines who concedes first.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: In bilateral negotiations with no competing alternatives on either side, the party with the less-attractive BATNA loses leverage; the party more willing to walk away forces concessions.
bounded_by: Assumes neither party has alternative options (no competing buyers, no alternative properties)

examples.text: In home buying: Hormozi and his partner Layla wanted to buy a specific home. Hormozi's BATNA was to do nothing and keep the home they already owned and liked. The sellers' BATNA was to continue holding an aggressively priced property with no competing offers. Hormozi knew he was in a strong position because the sellers had not received other bids, and his current home was performing well as a backup plan. This allowed him to negotiate confidently from a position of genuine indifference to the outcome.

In inventory sales: If a buyer offers $10 per unit for inventory and you know you have other buyers willing to purchase at the same price, your BATNA is to sell to the alternative buyer. Instead of accepting $10, you can counter at $10.50 or $11 because you know the deal will happen either way. But if you know the deal is not guaranteed, you should accept $10 to ensure the sale happens.

practices.text: Before any negotiation, establish your BATNA by identifying your true alternative (continuing your existing situation, walking away, or choosing an alternative option). This work must be done before sitting down at the table.
When purchasing, get multiple quotes from vendors before deciding on a partner. Obtaining 4-5 competitive bids educates you on industry standards and provides negotiating leverage.

Never accept the first offer without comparing it to alternatives. Even if one negotiation produces an attractive offer, comparing it to other available options determines whether the offer is truly competitive.
In employment negotiation, only negotiate with your current employer when you already have another job offer. This gives you concrete leverage in the form of a competing option.
When you have strong BATNA, project confidence in negotiation. Your psychological belief that you will succeed either way changes the dynamic and allows you to ask for more aggressive concessions.
